read_scope.notes: Read the complete 22-page frozen PDF, including references and Appendices A–G. Visually inspected every rendered page, all five figures and all twelve tables. Consulted the frozen paper.tex and specificity_results.tex for exact wording, notation and locations. Independently computed the supplied PDF SHA256. Checked that the abstract contains 155 whitespace-delimited words after TeX accent and punctuation normalization. Extraction and rendering used an isolated /tmp/editorial-r28-a.F7ufvp directory. No other review records or manuscript versions were consulted.

score_reasons.expression: Excellent, precise English with unusually good control of consequential qualifications. Sections 4.1–4.2 define contrasts, alignment and error in plain language before equations; the lightness example and the 1/0/1 error examples make the terminology concrete. Sentences are generally manageable, and primary results consistently distinguish point estimates from resolved comparisons. The abstract compresses the calibration explanation into an order that briefly makes the reader decode the ranking before understanding the operation; a little repetition remains in the final synthesis.
score_reasons.structure: The question, common-scene design, measured features, score interpretation and results form a coherent progression. Results 5.1–5.5 move from primary agreement to the shared response, painter pairs, calibration and source sensitivity. Retrospective status is explicit in Section 4.4 and the relevant tables, while derivations and earlier cohorts are appropriately optional appendices. The short Discussion mostly reiterates conclusions already established; replacing its opening summary with a more integrated explanation would improve the final payoff without changing the structure or adding length.
score_reasons.new_reader_understanding: The manuscript is understandable without repository consultation. The six arms and reference target are explicit, Table 1 explains feature families, Section 4.1 supplies numerical intuition, and captions give interpretable benchmarks. The distinction between a theoretical no-contrast predictor and the observed generic-painting arm is especially useful. Calibration and fixed-scene uncertainty are adequately explained in the main text. A remaining localized ambiguity is that the headline shared-change percentage can be too readily equated with the generic-painting effect, even though it includes any response common to the named clauses and the generic shift is separately measured.
score_reasons.engagement: The concrete Monet/Sisley motivation, the inspectable six-by-six image panel, and the contrasting GPT Image 2/FLUX examples give the paper a discernible and consequential narrative. Figure 3 rewards inspection by making weak Monet–Sisley responses immediately visible. The main narrative maintains a reasonable pace despite necessary statistical distinctions. Figure 2 is crowded at normal page scale, and the Discussion offers less interpretive payoff than the strong result sections could support.

strengths: Section 4.1 uses an actual median-lightness contrast and three idealized error values to establish the geometry before notation.
The central result is stated precisely: all models have positive reference-aligned responses, but none is established to beat the no-distinction error benchmark.
Figure 1 presents every model and condition for a clearly identified scene, with reference examples explicitly separated from matched inputs or perceptual validation.
Sections 5.3–5.4 explain why greater alignment, lower total error and lower calibrated error need not select the same model; numerical examples support each distinction.
Source correction is presented transparently through Table 5, including the changed Sunburst comparison and the retrospective status of corrected intervals.
Technical appendices preserve detailed estimators and supporting cohorts without making them prerequisites for following the main study.

findings.issue: The reader encounters the uncalibrated/held-out model ranking before the abstract explains what calibration does. Within an otherwise standalone abstract, this creates a brief concentration of undefined procedure terms.
findings.reader_effect: A new reader may initially read the changed ranking as a result of modifying or improving images and must revise that interpretation in the next sentence.
findings.suggested_change: Replace the ranking and definition sentences, at equal or shorter length, with wording that introduces the operation first: “Retrospectively fitting one scale factor per model on other scenes gives GPT Image 2 the lowest held-out error estimate; FLUX.2 Max has the lowest uncalibrated scene error. This rescales measured contrasts without changing images.” Keep the abstract at or below 155 words.

findings.location: Section 5.2 and Table 3, page 8; specificity_results.tex lines 43–54
findings.issue: The text defines the shared named-minus-artist-free component correctly, but “including the painting clause” leaves its relationship to the separately measured generic-painting arm slightly implicit. The 82.5–95.7% statistic is not a decomposition attributing that percentage specifically to the generic clause.
findings.reader_effect: Because the generic control and the shared painting response are central to the motivation, readers can too readily interpret the headline percentage as the fraction explained by the generic-painting arm.
findings.suggested_change: Replace the opening definition with an equally compact clarification: “After averaging scenes, we separate change common to all named prompts—including the painting clause and any common naming response—from differences among names.” Preserve the subsequent generic-arm comparison as a distinct result; no additional analysis or paragraph is needed.

findings.issue: Six overview plots plus six narrow detail plots place many ticks, markers and M/S/P labels in one compact figure. The detail panels are useful, but nearby circles and reference labels require close inspection at normal page scale.
findings.reader_effect: The figure communicates the Cézanne separation quickly, while the more consequential Monet/Sisley differences take more effort to decode than the adjacent heatmap.
findings.suggested_change: Within the existing figure area, remove redundant interior tick labels and use the freed space to enlarge the detail panels or increase their marker/letter separation. Retain common scales and the complete model and painter coverage.

findings.issue: The opening Discussion paragraph largely restates the result headings, and the next paragraph immediately turns to unidentified mechanisms. It gives little additional synthesis before the limitations and conclusion.
findings.reader_effect: After the strong sequence of numerical reversals, the ending has less explanatory payoff than the results themselves.
findings.suggested_change: Replace the opening paragraph with a short synthesis of the existing evidence: positive overall alignment establishes a measured name response; painter-pair checks show whether that response covers the intended distinctions; the scene and calibration comparisons show why low error alone does not answer both questions. Keep the replacement within the current paragraph length and retain the bounded digital-reference interpretation.

summary: An excellent and largely self-contained account of a bounded digital-reference comparison. The central distinctions are readily understood, the primary/retrospective hierarchy is clear, and the paper avoids unsupported perceptual claims. Remaining changes are localized editorial refinements, not a need for new experiments or a different feature representation.
